quals-wisconsin-algebra-1991s-01.title: Permutation representation and the Frattini argument
quals-wisconsin-algebra-1991s-01.body:
Let $P\in\mathrm{Syl}_p(G)$ and $N=N_G(P)$, so $|G:N|=n$. The conjugation action of $G$ on the $n$-element set $\mathrm{Syl}_p(G)$ (equivalently, the action on the cosets of $N$) gives a homomorphism $\pi\colon G\to\mathrm{Sym}_n$ whose kernel $K=\bigcap_g N^g$ is contained in $N$. Put $H=\pi(G)\cong G/K$, a subgroup of $\mathrm{Sym}_n$. Write $\bar X=XK/K$.

$\bar P=PK/K$ is a Sylow $p$-subgroup of $\bar G$ (its index $|G:PK|$ divides $|G:P|$, which is prime to $p$). The number of Sylow $p$-subgroups of $\bar G$ is $|\bar G:N_{\bar G}(\bar P)|$. By the correspondence theorem $N_{\bar G}(\bar P)=\bar M$ where $M=N_G(PK)$, and $|\bar G:\bar M|=|G:M|$ since $K\subseteq M$.

We claim $M=N$. Since $K\trianglelefteq G$ and $P\le N$, $N$ normalizes $PK$, so $N\subseteq M$. Conversely $PK\trianglelefteq M$ and $P$ is a Sylow $p$-subgroup of $PK$, so the Frattini argument gives $M=N_M(P)\,PK\subseteq N\cdot PK=N$ (as $P,K\subseteq N$).

Therefore $H=\bar G\le\mathrm{Sym}_n$ has exactly $|G:N|=n$ Sylow $p$-subgroups. ∎

quals-wisconsin-algebra-1991s-02.title: Nullstellensatz and reduction mod 3
quals-wisconsin-algebra-1991s-02.body:
**(a)** Let $S=\mathbb C[x_1,\dots,x_n]$ and let $M$ be a maximal ideal of $S$ containing the proper ideal $I$. Then $S/M$ is a field which is finitely generated as a $\mathbb C$-algebra, so by Zariski's lemma (the weak Nullstellensatz) it is a finite, hence algebraic, extension of $\mathbb C$; as $\mathbb C$ is algebraically closed, the natural map $\mathbb C\to S/M$ is an isomorphism. Let $a_i\in\mathbb C$ correspond to $x_i+M$. The composite $\phi\colon S\to S/M\cong\mathbb C$ is a $\mathbb C$-algebra homomorphism with $\phi(x_i)=a_i$, so $\phi=\phi_a$. Thus $\ker\phi_a=M\supseteq I$, and $\phi_a(I)=0\ne\mathbb C$.

**(b)** Reduction mod $3$ followed by the quotient map gives a surjective ring homomorphism
$$\mathbb Z[x]\to\mathbb F_3[x]\to\mathbb F_3[x]/(x^2+1)$$
whose kernel contains $3$ and $x^2+1$, hence $I$. The target is nonzero (in fact $x^2+1$ has no root in $\mathbb F_3$, so it is the field $\mathbb F_9$), so $I\ne\mathbb Z[x]$.

Now fix $a\in\mathbb Z$. Since $\phi_a$ is surjective, $\phi_a(I)$ is an ideal of $\mathbb Z$; it contains $\phi_a(3)=3$ and $\phi_a(x^2+1)=a^2+1$. Squares mod $3$ are $0$ and $1$, so $a^2+1\equiv1$ or $2\pmod 3$ and $3\nmid a^2+1$. The ideal $\phi_a(I)\supseteq 3\mathbb Z$ is therefore $3\mathbb Z$ or $\mathbb Z$, and it is not $3\mathbb Z$; hence $\phi_a(I)=\mathbb Z$. ∎

quals-wisconsin-algebra-1991s-03.title: Separability, degrees and the Galois correspondence
quals-wisconsin-algebra-1991s-03.body:
**(a)** For $\gamma\in E$, the minimal polynomial $m_\gamma$ of $\gamma$ over $F$ has degree $d\mid 4$, so $d\in\{1,2,4\}$. Its derivative has leading coefficient $d\cdot1\ne0$ because $\mathrm{char}F\ne2$, so $\gcd(m_\gamma,m_\gamma')=1$ ($m_\gamma$ is irreducible and $m_\gamma'\ne0$ has smaller degree). Hence every element is separable, $E/F$ is a finite separable extension, and the primitive element theorem gives $E=F[\alpha]$.

**(b)** $\alpha^2$ is a root of $y^2+ay+b\in F[y]$, so $|F[\alpha^2]:F|\le2$; and $\alpha$ is a root of $x^2-\alpha^2\in F[\alpha^2][x]$, so $|F[\alpha]:F[\alpha^2]|\le2$. Since the product of these degrees is $|E:F|=4$, both equal $2$, and $F[\alpha^2]$ lies properly between $F$ and $E$.

**(c)** Let $m$ be the minimal polynomial of $\beta$, of degree $4$. Since the extension is separable (by (a)), $L/F$ is Galois, and $|L:F|=|\mathrm{Gal}(L/F)|=24$. By the Galois correspondence, $E=L^H$ for a subgroup $H\le G=\mathrm{Gal}(L/F)\cong\mathrm{Sym}_4$ with $|G:H|=|E:F|=4$, i.e. $|H|=6$, and intermediate fields $F\subsetneq K\subsetneq E$ correspond to subgroups $H\subsetneq J\subsetneq G$.

Such a $J$ would have order $12$ (a proper multiple of $6$ dividing $24$). The only subgroup of order $12$ in $\mathrm{Sym}_4$ is $\mathrm{Alt}_4$ (a subgroup of index 2 contains all squares, in particular all $3$-cycles, which generate $\mathrm{Alt}_4$). But $\mathrm{Alt}_4$ has no subgroup of order $6$: such a subgroup would have index $2$, hence be normal and contain the squares of all elements, i.e. all eight $3$-cycles — too many for a group of order 6. So no $J$ exists and $H$ is maximal; there is no field properly between $F$ and $E$. ∎

Set $v_i=B^{i-1}v$ for $i=1,\dots,p$. By induction $v_i$ is an eigenvector of $A$ with eigenvalue $\mu+i-1$. The elements $\mu,\mu+1,\dots,\mu+p-1$ of $F$ are distinct (they differ by $1,\dots,p-1$, nonzero in characteristic $p$), and eigenvectors for distinct eigenvalues are linearly independent. Since $\dim V=p$, $\{v_1,\dots,v_p\}$ is a basis of $V$, and $Bv_i=v_{i+1}$ for $i<p$ by construction.

Finally, $Bv_p$ is a nonzero eigenvector of $A$ with eigenvalue $\mu+p=\mu$. In the eigenbasis $v_1,\dots,v_p$ with distinct eigenvalues, the $\mu$-eigenspace is $Fv_1$, so $Bv_p=\lambda v_1$ with $\lambda

quals-wisconsin-algebra-1991s-05.title: Compare cyclic subgroups
quals-wisconsin-algebra-1991s-05.body:
**(a)** Let $x,y\in G$. Then $\langle x\rangle\subseteq\langle y\rangle$ or $\langle y\rangle\subseteq\langle x\rangle$; either way one is a power of the other, so $xy=yx$. Hence $G$ is abelian.

If $x$ had infinite order, then $\langle x^2\rangle$ and $\langle x^3\rangle$ would be incomparable: $x^2\in\langle x^3\rangle$ would mean $x^2=x^{3k}$, i.e. $2=3k$, and $x^3\in\langle x^2\rangle$ would mean $3=2k$. So every element has finite order.

Since $G\ne1$, some element has order divisible by a prime $p$. If primes $p\ne q$ divide $o(x)$ and $o(y)$ respectively, then $\langle x\rangle$ contains a subgroup $X$ of order $p$ and $\langle y\rangle$ a subgroup $Y$ of order $q$, and neither of $X,Y$ contains the other (orders $p\nmid q$, $q\nmid p$). Thus only one prime $p$ divides element orders, and all orders are powers of $p$.

**(b)** $G_n$ is a subgroup since $G$ is abelian. Let $H\le G_n$ be finite. By the fundamental theorem of finite abelian groups, $H$ is a direct product of cyclic groups; two nontrivial factors $C_1,C_2$ would be incomparable subgroups ($C_1\cap C_2=1$). So $H$ is cyclic, and since $h^{p^n}=1$ for all $h\in H$, $|H|\le p^n$.

Every finitely generated subgroup of the abelian torsion group $G_n$ is finite, so $G_n$ is the union of its finite subgroups. If $|G_n|>p^n$, pick $p^n+1$ distinct elements; they generate a finite subgroup of order $>p^n$, a contradiction. Hence $|G_n|\le p^n$. ∎
